The wounded man was taken to the office of Dr. Harry Todd, in the Central Office building, but the bullet could not be located. It is believed that it struck the bone, and was turned away from a straight course. The revolver was a 38-calibre bull-dog. The shoot occurred at the corner of Market and Main sts. him. Forbes lives at 120 Ohio st.

When arraigned in Mayor's court Monday morning, Howard pleaded not guilty. The case was continued to Wednesday morning, bond being fixed at $1,000. The charge is "shooting" with intent to wound."

ESCAPED THE MOB. Hundreds of People After a Negro at Akron, O. Akron, O., Aug. 13. There came near being a lynching in Akron tonight, and only the fleetness of a negro—Bud Howard—in getting away from a howling mob saved him from being killed. In an altercation with a white man named John Forbes, Howard pulled a revolver and shot Forbes, Forbes sank to the ground wounded. This was at the corner of Main and Market streets, the busiest corner in the city, and a crowd gathered in a minute. Hundreds of men started after Howard, yelling "Lynch him!" Howard had a few hundred feet the start, and finally got away. He was afterward captured by the police while boarding a freight train in East Akron. Forbes was wounded in the thigh and will recover. STEVEDORES STRIKE. Two Thousand Men in Baltimore Engage in a Riot—Several Are Wounded.
Baltimore, Aug. 13.—The strike of the 2,000 union stevedores who went out last week is assuming an ugly aspect and minor disturbances are of daily occurrence. A big crowd last night attacked a street car at Locust Point, in which were a number of non-union colored men who had taken the strikers' places, and bombarded it with bricks and other missiles until dispersed by the police. Tonight they attacked a gang of fifteen colored men as the latter emerged from the Baltimore and Ohio docks at Locust Point, following them several blocks and pelting them with stones and bricks.

At the foot of Allen street one of the negroes drew a pistol and fired five shots into the crowd. Three of the shots took effect, wounding Henry Presser, Joseph Benesch and Arthur Ranier. None of the wounds are serious, and the man who did the shooting, together with his companions, fled, and has not yet been arrested.

DYNAMITE IS SECURED.
Akron, 0., Aug. 23.—It has just been reported that a mob forced an entrance into a pottery and secured a large quantity of dynamite and that this will be thrown among the troops tonight. Feeling is still running high and a leader would probably cause further depredations. About forty rioters broke into the Standard company's store, about 11 o'clock, smashing a big plate-glass window. Later fully 500 returned to the store for more weapons. Policemen and employes of the store were held at bay across the street while the store was looted. Akron, O., Aug. 23.—As a result of last night's riot, two are dead, two will die, sixteen others are more or less injured, and fully a million dollars in property has gone up in smoke. The city hall is totally destroyed, the Columbian building, which adjoined the city hall, is a heap of ashes, and several smaller frame buildings in the vicinity are in ruins. The destruction was wrought by the wild mob which held possession of the city from dark until almost dawn this morning. It is said the mob was composed of not less than 1500 men. shot in foot. Nearly 5000 persons surrounded the city prison early in the evening clamoring for the negro. Fearing trouble, Peek and Bud Howard, another negro under arrest for shooting John Forbes, were sent to Cleveland. Assurance that Peck was not in the prison failed to satisfy the mob. With a rush it broke open a door, and pushing by a helpless squad of policemen, went through the building. At last the leaders were persuaded to allow a committee to make careful search, while the others retired. When the committee reported that Peck was not there the crowd made a rush for the jail, but failed to find the object of its search. The mob was composed chiefly of workingmen, including about 500 who had assembled on Perkins' hill, the house of Tina Maas, and went in a body to the prison, headed by the little girl's father. Persuaded at last that Peck had been taken away, the mob still refused to disperse, and a negro who passed by ran a gauntlet of kicks and cuffs. Peck is 35 years old and has a family. During the day Peck confessed to Prisonkeeper Washer that he had attempted to assault the girl, who is the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Theodore Maas, industrious and respectable people, who live on Perkins hill. On Monday night he offered to give the child a ride in his buggy. Christina accepted the invitation and a few hours later she was found on the side of a road west of the city. In the police court he pleaded guilty and was bound over to the common pleas court, his bail being placed at $5000. The story of his confession spread like wildfire throughout the city, and officers learned that an attempt would be made to lynch him. Peck was badly frightened, and was greatly relieved when he learned he was to be taken out of the town Thousands of people came to this city today to see the ruins of the buildings destroyed by the mob last night. Cleveland, O., Aug. 23.—Louis Peck, the alleged rapist, whose life the Akron mob so eagerly sought last night, is locked up in the county jail in this city. Peck was very reticent about his arrest. More information was obtained from Howard, who was brought to Cleveland because it was feared that the angry populace would not stop to inquire whether Howard had been in jail two months or not, as he says he had. In answer to questions Peck said he is 36 years old, married and has one child. Howard said: "I do not want you to mix me up in this affair as I was in jail before Peck was arrested, awaiting my case. I was taken out of jail because the sheriff felt no colored man would be safe there." Confession was obtained from Peck by Deputy Sheriff Barry at the county jail here today. Peck said that he had attempted to assault the girl but was very sorry for it. He attributed his act to liquor. He said that he had been on a spree for a month.

bud-howard-akron-1900-08-13.A8:
FEARS TO TO RETURN.
Bud Howard Wants to be Tried Somewhere Else.
"Bud" Howard, the negro who was brought to Cleveland recently with Louis Peck to escape the vengeance of a mob at Akron, is still confined in the county jail, says the Leader. He is under arrest on the charge of shooting to wound. It is claimed he shot a man in the foot.

It is now known what will be done with Howard. He is anxious that his case be tried anywhere but at Akron. He receives no visitors and is allowed no more privileges than the ordinary prisoner. He looks none the worse for the excitement which he has been under incident to the stirring times which occurred at Akron.

Death of the Well-Known Divine at the Home of His Son in Syracuse, N. Y. Syracuse, N. Y., July 31.—Rev. William Dexter Wilson, D.D., LL.D., died at his son's home in this city of old age. He was born in Stoddard, N. H., in 1816, was graduated from the Harvard divinity school in 1838; was for three years a Unitarian preacher, and then joined the Episcopal church. He was professor in Geneva college (now Hobart) from 1850 to 1868, leaving there at the request of his former pupil, Andrew D. White, to become registrar of Cornell university and professor of moral philosophy. Since 1886 he has been emeritus professor of Cornell and head of St. Andrews divinity school of this city. EXPECTS A BIG STRIKE. The Trust Mills Refuse the Demands for More Pay, and 24,000 Puddlers May Go Out. Cincinnati, July 31.—Charles H. Davis, of Newport, Ky., vice president of the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers, stated Monday that a strike of 24,000 puddlers in the United States is probable. They demanded an increase of from $5 to $5.50 a tap, and the committees from the union and employers had failed to agree. The independent mills are willing to grant the demands, but the trust holds out. "We have given them 30 days, which will expire in about two weeks, to grant our demands," said Davis, "or a general strike will be ordered." Race War at Donivan, Mo.
Popular Bluffs, Mo., July 29.—The importation of a large number of Negroes in Donivan nearly precipitated a race war. No Negroes are allowed to live in the town, and on their arrival the citizens undertook to drive them out. Several colored men were roughly handled, and a number of white men and Negroes were injured. Sheriff Merrill came to the rescue and an armed posse is now guarding the colored laborers. The citizens are determined the Negroes shall not be allowed to remain and further trouble is expected.

Tod Sloan Hurt.

Liverpool, England, July 28.—In the race for the Liverpool cup Tod Sloan was badly injured. He rode Maluma, who slipped and fell, throwing Sloan violently to the ground. He was badly cut about the head. One ear was torn and he was much shaken and bruised. No internal injuries are believed to have been received that will prevent him from filling his engagements in the United States. It is thought the fall will end Maluma's racing career, as it put her shoulder out.

Richard D. Yelland, the distinguished landscape artist, died of pneumonia at his home in San Francisco, aged 52 years.

REIGN OF TERROR IN FLORIDA
AMONG NEGROES.
Masked Men Fire Into Ranks of Laborers and Dangerously Wounded Three.
A special from Pensacola, Fla., says: In the hope that those concerned might be apprehended, a terrible state of affairs in Washington, county, Fla., has been kept quiet, and just now made public.

For some time, indiscriminate shooting and attempts to murder have been of almost daily occurrence near Chipley, the county seat of Washington county.

Last Thursday night, however, a climax was reached when about a dozen masked men proceeded to the quarters of a turpentine camp, and, calling out the occupants, who were mostly negroes, fired several volleys from Winchester rifles and shotguns in their midst.

One negro was instantly killed and four dangerously wounded, two of whom are reported as having died Monday morning.

The firing was kept up for several minutes, but no one else was hit, as at the first volley, a l ran back and barred the doors and windows, thus escaping a wholesale killing.

The coroner's jury verdict was that the dead negro met his death from gunshot wounds, inflicted by unknown parties. Two farmers are suspected and have been jailed.

The arrest of two suspects was thought to have had a quieting effect on the lawless element, but such is not the case. Saturday morning, while a white man was at his post of duty in the turpentine district, he was suddenly confronted by a man in disguise, and told to "move on, and not come back." Failing to "move" as fast as his unwelcome visitor would wish, a few shots were fired, which had the desired effect of electrifying him.

The work of lawlessness has been so open and promiscuous that help is hard to obtain, and the turpentine operations are experiencing much trouble in operating their stills. It is said the whites in that neighborhood have a deadly hatred for negroes and are determined to either drive them from that vicinity or exterminate them altogether.

WINCHESTER, VA., August 29.—Incoming delegates by the score made the second day's session of the Virginia Young People's Society of Christian Endeavor the largest in the convention history of the State organization. The town is practically turned over to them.

The convention held three sessions in Centenary Reformed Church. At the morning session H. R. Thomas read a paper on "The Responsibility of Leading a Meeting." President R. E. Hutton read his annual report, which showed gratifying success in the growth of the society during the past year.

The report of Miss Lula O. Phillips, of Richmond, the State Secretary, showed the following number of societies in the State's Union to be 233; total membership, 10,000. In the State Union twelve different churches are represented, while thirty are Union societies and three are not connected with any church. CHURCHES REPRESENTED.

Among the churches represented in the Union are the Disciples, 56 societies; Presbyterians, 40; Baptists, 19; Methodist Episcopal Church, Protestant, 16; Metodist Episcopal, North and South, 16; United Brethren, 8; Christian, 7; Reformed, 4; Episcopal, 3; Congregational, 1; Friends, 1.

Treasurer H. F. Lowe, of Falls Church, reported the financial condition of the Union to be in excellent shape, with largely increased receipts.

Rev. Dr. H. P. Hamill, of Trinity Church, Lexington, delivered an address on "Present Day Problems for Christian Endeavorers." The report of the committee appointed to secure a State song for the use of the Union excited considerable discussion. The old committee was discharged and a new one, consisting of Prof. E. T. The leading feature of the afternoon session was the address by Prof. James Lewis Howe, of Washington and Lee University, on "Denominational riteny and Inter-Denominational Fellowship." Other addresses were also made by Rev. Charles M. Compher, D. D., of Baltimore, Md., on "Saved for Service"; Rev. C. W. Frauck, Buena Vista; W. W. Douglas, of Ballston, and Miss Lillie Pearce, of Richmond, At night Rev. Ellis S. Hay, of Roanoke, addressed the convention on "Some Spiritual Triumphs of the Nineteenth Century," and Rev. F. D. Power, LL. D., of Washington, D. C., talked on the "Mastery of Jesus." The standing committees were announced at the afternoon session.

RACE RIOT.

A small riot between whites and negroes occurred here this morning while a circus was unloading. A white boy and a colored boy were fighting, and when a white man attempted to stop them, a burly negro interfered. A free fight ensued with a number of whites on one side and negroes on the other side. William Custy, white, acting as peace-maker, was knocked unconscious by William Pratt, a negro, with brass knuckles. Thinking Custy was killed, the negroes fled, pursued by the whites, and have eluded capture. Custy was badly hurt, and several negroes were severely beaten up.

The young twin daughters of Raymond Carver, of Red Bud, were buried in the same coffin at that place this afternoon. They died within a short time of each other on yesterday.

Briefs.
August has gone, but the hot weather still remains. It is said that the duration and intensity of the heated spell throughout the month of August has been without precedent, especially is this true in some of the cities. The heat, no doubt, has something to do with the prevalence of typhoid in the county; we understand there are a number of cases of this disease in the county and a great many threatened with an attack of same.

Received by Baughman another lot of Novelties in Jewelry. Get our prices before making your purchase.

The Winchester Star says: Last week Lake View experienced some excitement. R. P. Cline, the village blacksmith, claims he was tantalized and irritated beyond endurance by a boy, John Stewart. Cline shot at the boy and missed. The boy ran home it is said, secured a gun, rushed back and shot at Cline. A small amount of skin was knocked from the latter's finger, but no serious damage resulted.

The Winchester Times tells of a shipper in peaches who lost by his operation. He was a "small shipper," so called. He bought 56 bushels from a grower, crated them and sent them to a Pittsburg commission merchant. The peaches were sold, commission and freight charges deducted, and check for shipper's share transmitted. It was $1.86. Commission merchant's explanation: "Market glutted."

What promised to be a serious riot broke out in Winchester Wednesday last while Sparks' Circus was being unloaded. Trouble was precipitated by several small boys fighting, which resulted in a small race war, in which William Custy was struck with a black-jack in the hands of a negro and seriously injured. Will Pratt, Custy's assailant, fled, but has since been apprehended.

The Winchester Box Factory has been organized at Winchester with John C. Grove as manager. Paper boxes and other pasteboard articles will be manufactured in sufficient quantities to meet the home consumption. Winchester's Board of Trade recently organized, is certainly doing effective work, as this, we think, is the third manufacturing enterprise that has been located in that city through its influence.

Mr. J. S. Coleman, of Summit Point, carried off the ribbon and 1st money for the best pair of horses at the Inwood Fair. Jim has ever loved fine horses and admired pretty women. He always manages to have some of the former and acknowledges himself a candidate for the latter. — Charlestown Advocate.
